=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

## Overall assessment

**Do not accept the package as drafted.** It combines broad exclusions of liability with unresolved completion risks. The most important buyer protections concern Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay IP, transaction-related payments and the scope of the Seller’s liability.

This review is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter—not the full SPA or underlying DD documents. The recommendations below are buyer negotiating positions, not assertions that any particular term is universally “market”.

## 1. Liability provisions substantially weaken the Buyer’s remedies

### General cap, thresholds and time limits

The proposed general warranty package comprises:

- **AUD 4.8 million cap**—20% of the price;
- claims must **exceed AUD 25,000**;
- **AUD 250,000 deductible basket**—only the excess is recoverable; and
- notification within **18 months**.

These protections operate cumulatively. The Buyer could suffer significant losses yet recover little or nothing, particularly where losses comprise several smaller claims.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher general cap and a longer notification period, covering at least two full post-completion financial reporting cycles.
- Reduce the de minimis and basket; seek a **tipping basket**, under which the full qualifying amount becomes recoverable once the threshold is crossed.
- Aggregate claims arising from the same or related facts when applying thresholds.
- Ensure timely notified claims survive expiry, with workable notification requirements and no unduly short deadline for commencing proceedings.

### Fundamental warranties must have separate protection

Applying the general cap and 18-month period to capacity and title is unacceptable from the Buyer’s perspective. If the Seller cannot validly transfer the shares, recovering only 20% of the price is inadequate.

**Push back:** Separate capacity, authority, ownership and unencumbered title warranties, with a cap of at least the purchase price and a substantially longer claim period. Fraud should not benefit from contractual caps or exclusions, subject to applicable law and carefully drafted attribution provisions.

### “All Claims” language is especially dangerous

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5, together with the proposed universal time-limit rule, could extend warranty limitations to:
- specific indemnities and tax claims;
- repayment, price adjustment and other payment obligations;
- completion and post-completion covenants; and
- misrepresentation or other non-contractual claims.

**Push back:** Define expressly which limitations apply to each claim category. Do not allow general warranty limitations to restrict specific indemnities, purchase-price mechanics or performance obligations by default. Preserve fraud remedies and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions against the complete SPA; they are substantive risk transfers, not administrative drafting.

## 2. Disclosure and deemed knowledge could hollow out the warranties

General disclosure of the entire data room, material merely “referred to”, public records and statutory registers is too broad. Clause 8.3 goes further by treating matters **discoverable** by the Buyer or its advisers as known.

Together, these provisions could defeat claims even where the relevant problem was obscure, incomplete or never actually understood.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter** and the warranties affected.
- Reject constructive knowledge and blanket attribution of advisers’ knowledge.
- If a knowledge exclusion is unavoidable, confine it to the actual conscious knowledge of named Buyer personnel at an agreed date.
- Freeze and retain the disclosure record, with an agreed index and accessible copies. The 22 September 2026 snapshot also needs updating appropriately before signing/completion.
- State that disclosure and knowledge do not qualify specific indemnities or completion obligations unless expressly agreed.

A disclosed risk is not necessarily an accepted risk. Known issues often need **stronger contractual protection**, because ordinary warranty recovery may be unavailable.

## 3. Bluefen consent is a critical completion condition

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The supplied material contains neither final written consent nor evidence that its associated conditions have been satisfied.

“Reasonable endeavours” is only an efforts obligation. Delivery of a consent document is not sufficient if it is conditional, ineffective, revocable or requires commercially adverse concessions.

**Push back:**
- Require an effective written consent satisfying clauses 11.2 and 11.3, with associated conditions satisfied or appropriately waived.
- Make acceptable consent a condition precedent for the Buyer’s benefit, waivable only by the Buyer.
- Prohibit material amendments, fees or concessions without Buyer approval.
- Include a long-stop date and termination rights.

Do not treat this issue as resolved on the present evidence.

## 4. Riverlark repayment and security release must occur at completion

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding. A release supplied after completion leaves the acquired company exposed to lender rights and security enforcement, inconsistent with the debt-free/cash-free baseline.

**Push back:**
- Obtain an up-to-date lender payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and all secured obligations.
- Provide for repayment through the completion funds flow and effective release of security and guarantees at completion.
- Obtain agreed release documents, lender undertakings and arrangements for registering discharges.
- Resolve any change-of-control requirements if the facility remains outstanding when control changes.

The debt must be reflected consistently in the price and funds flow—normally by directing the relevant portion of Seller proceeds to repayment—not added to the Buyer’s agreed economic cost or deducted twice.

## 5. Ironquay presents an IP ownership risk, not merely an unpaid invoice

Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, but does not independently prove the current payment position. No payment receipt or confirmatory assignment is supplied.

An indemnity limited to the specific payment may not cover the consequences of missing IP rights, including infringement allegations, remediation or interruption to commercial use.

**Push back:**
- Verify all SOW3 amounts and obtain cleared-payment evidence.
- Require an effective confirmatory assignment/release and verify the relevant chain of ownership.
- Make resolution a completion deliverable—or condition if the IP is business-critical.
- Broaden the specific indemnity to cover losses arising from pre-completion non-payment or defective ownership, rather than merely reimbursing an invoice. Give it express protection from general disclosure, knowledge and warranty limitations.

## 6. Completion bonuses must be allocated and funded expressly

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional on completion and continued employment, but absent from the funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the acquired company becoming liable.

**Push back:**
- Verify the payment triggers, timing and continued-employment conditions.
- Allocate the transaction-triggered cost expressly to the Seller, through payment, an appropriate price adjustment or a specific indemnity.
- Determine associated superannuation, payroll tax and other employer on-costs.
- Coordinate the treatment with debt-like items and working capital to prevent omissions or double counting.

Distinguish sale-triggered bonuses from any genuinely post-completion retention arrangement the Buyer separately chooses to fund.

## 7. The export/privacy incident requires investigation and tailored protection

The evidence establishes an unintended external delivery of a download link. It does **not** establish access, the exact affected data, a confirmed reportable breach or quantified loss. Equally, the Seller’s assertion that it is unlikely to be material is unsupported by a completed investigation.

**Push back:**
- Obtain access logs, link permissions and expiry details, containment evidence, recipient communications and a verified data inventory.
- Require a documented assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations.
- Require prompt updates, evidence preservation and appropriate Buyer consultation, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for losses attributable to the pre-completion incident, with suitable coverage and duration.

If diligence shows significant unresolved exposure, consider a holdback or a completion condition. Do not assume either that notification is required or that it is unnecessary.

## 8. Supplier renewals require classification—not automatic acceptance or deduction

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Neither “ordinary-course operating costs” nor automatic debt-like treatment is established.

**Push back:** Read DD-008 and DD-011 together and verify execution dates, service periods, cancellation rights, accruals and whether the commitments were authorised. Then allocate them consistently under working capital, debt-like items and pre-completion conduct restrictions. Ordinary future operating expenditure should not automatically reduce price; exceptional, overdue or transaction-related liabilities may warrant different treatment.

## 9. Tax and IP are not adequately resolved by calling them “settled”

**Tax:** Seek a dedicated pre-completion tax indemnity, appropriate allocation rules and claims-control provisions. Negotiate separate caps and periods aligned with relevant assessment and amendment exposure, plus a claims buffer—not the general 18-month regime.

**IP:** Retain meaningful ownership, licensing and infringement warranties alongside the Ironquay-specific solution. Assess whether core IP exposure warrants separate limits or longer survival. A specific Ironquay indemnity is not a substitute for wider IP protection.

## 10. Title and other contractual requirements need proportionate verification

- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, not complete verification. Check valid issuance, the ownership chain, encumbrances, options, convertible securities, transfer restrictions and required approvals. Completion must deliver valid transfer and registration of 100% of the shares, free of encumbrances.
- **Office lease:** The supplied material identifies notification, not landlord consent. Require compliance with the actual notification obligation; do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not itself establish that a share sale requires consent. Review the full contract for any separate change-of-control provision before requiring consent.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Protect completion:** Effective Bluefen consent; Riverlark repayment and release; satisfactory Ironquay ownership evidence.
2. **Fix the economics:** Express treatment of debt, bonuses and on-costs, with verified supplier classifications and no double counting.
3. **Preserve remedies:** Separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; narrow universal limitations, disclosure and deemed knowledge.
4. **Resolve uncertainty:** Complete incident diligence and obtain tailored protection.
5. **Secure recovery:** Assess Seller covenant strength and consider escrow, holdback or a guarantee. An indemnity is only useful if enforceable against a creditworthy party.

**Bottom line:** The Seller’s package transfers unresolved operational, ownership and completion risks to Wattlebridge while materially restricting recovery. Neither the disclosure of those risks nor the Seller’s description of the package as balanced is a reason to accept them.
